newsitem.title: CHINA: China in row with Denmark, Netherlands over rights.
newsitem.headline: China in row with Denmark, Netherlands over rights.

text.p: China on Tuesday gave Denmark and the Netherlands a diplomatic slap on the wrist by postponing official visits in a row over their support for a U.N. resolution critical of Beijing's human rights record.

"China...will delay important exchanges of officials that are under discussion and halt exchanges and cooperation with Denmark on human rights," Chinese Foreign Ministry spokesman Shen Guofang told a news briefing in Beijing.
Shen did not elaborate on the exchanges and the Danish embassy in Beijing declined to comment.
In The Hague, the Dutch economic affairs ministry said China has postponed a Dutch trade mission to Beijing.
"This Chinese step must be linked to the role that the Netherlands...has played in drawing attention to human rights in China at the U.N. Human Rights Commission in Geneva," the Dutch ministry said.
The mission would have visited China from June 7 to 14 under the leadership of Economic Affairs Minister Hans Wijers.
Denmark, the Netherlands, the United States and 12 other countries are sponsoring a resolution at the United Nations Human Rights Commission in Geneva censuring Beijing for its human rights record.
China has warned that relations with these countries will be affected.
The resolution is due to come up for a vote in Geneva on Tuesday. China was expected to try to prevent debate on its human rights record by seeking approval of a motion of "no action".
Shen did not mention the Netherlands but he accused Denmark of interfering in China's internal affairs over its decision to present the resolution.

"Denmark...is interfering in China's internal affairs and hurting the feelings of the Chinese people," Shen said. Denmark "has set up obstacles to the smooth development of relations between the two countries".
"Sino-Danish relations have been damaged. This is something the Chinese side does not wish to see...The Chinese side cannot not react," Shen added.
China hoped Denmark would have a change of heart, he said.
"We sincerely hope...Denmark will change its confrontational method and return to the road of dialogue and cooperation on an equal footing."
The United States reaffirmed on Monday that it would give full backing to the resolution that called on China to observe human rights and protect the cultural identity of Tibetans.
Western groups have for years been critical of Beijing's handling of Tibet, which was seized by communist Chinese forces in 1950.

China, which says it has ruled Tibet for centuries, has allowed large numbers of ethnic Han Chinese to settle in the Himalayan region since the communists took power. That has raised concerns that Chinese culture was swamping the indigenous way of life.

Although U.S. officials privately expressed confidence that they would win good support, diplomats said a Chinese motion for "no action" on the resolution was likely to be passed easily -- as it was last year.
China, mainly with support from Asian and African members of the commission, has fought off European Union and U.S. efforts to have the U.N. body censure Beijing for the past six years in a row.
